newsitem.title: FRANCE: Council of Europe reaffirms Chechen invitations.
newsitem.headline: Council of Europe reaffirms Chechen invitations.

text.p: The Council of Europe, rejecting Russian criticism, on Thursday renewed invitations to the chief-of-staff of rebel Chechnya and Russian security boss Alexander Lebed to attend a hearing in Strasbourg.
In Moscow, President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky blasted the invitations as "rude interference in Russia's internal affairs".

"The question of future relations with the Chechen Republic will be decided by the president, the government and the legislature through talks," he told reporters. "We deem it inappropriate to discuss this issue at an international forum."
Leni Fischer, head of the Strasbourg Parliamentary Assembly of the 39-nation Council rejected charges the council was interfering in Moscow's domestic policies.
"Human rights violations are never an internal affair," he said.

"We invited the...two men who put an end to the fighting in Chechnya," Fischer said in a statement. He confirmed the invitation to Lebed and rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov to visit on September 23 and to take part in a hearing on their August 31 peace pact.
Russia joined the Council of Europe, which aims to foster democracy and human rights, in February only after Moscow pledged to seek a peaceful settlement in Chechnya.
The Council froze Russia's membership bid for most of 1995 in protest at the use of military force against civilians in the breakaway republic.
Fischer, a German, said: "There are many precedents for such a hearing, which in no way constitute a recognition of any legal status of the Chechen delegation."

In Moscow on Wednesday, Vladimir Lukin, liberal chairman of the Russian parliament's foreign affairs committee and head of Moscow's delegation to the Council, called the invitation "a rude, impertinent and unprecedented" interference.
The Interfax news agency quoted sources as saying Lukin and the Communist speaker of parliament wrote to the assembly saying Russia would not attend the planned session on September 23.

The peace deal signed after Moscow was humiliated by a rebel attack on Grozny provides for the withdrawal of all Russian troops temporarily stationed in the region and a delay in any discussion of the delicate issue of Chechnya's status.
